mobile.intro: A phone or tablet acts as a controller: it operates connected machines through the browser and does not run a terminal itself. Add tmex to the home screen for a full-screen, app-like experience.

computer.intro: After installing tmex on another server or computer, there are two ways to connect: join an existing relay (Hub), or make this machine the relay so other machines can join it.

install.title: Install tmex
install.description: Run the install script on the target machine (installs Bun automatically; Linux needs tmux ≥ 3.0). The terminal prints the access address when done.
install.pathHint: The install script provides the tmex command. If it is not found, reopen the terminal or run:

mode.title: Choose how to connect
mode.host: Use this machine as the relay

hub.title: Prepare the relay server
hub.description: Relay (Hub) needs a public HTTPS address; if none, set one up via "Use this machine as the relay".

token.title: Generate a join token
token.description: In the relay's tmex open Settings → Multi-node Mesh → Node management, click Add → Generate join token, then copy the join command. The token is valid for 10 minutes.
token.label: Join token (valid for {{minutes}} minutes)
token.meshDescription: Generate a join token here, then copy the command in the next step. The token is valid for 10 minutes.
token.unavailable: This machine is not part of a multi-node mesh, so a join token cannot be generated here.

run.title: Join from the new machine
run.description: Run the join command in the new machine's terminal (example below; use the command you copied):
run.ready: Run this command in the new machine's terminal:

confirm.title: Confirm the join
confirm.description: Back on the relay's Node management page, click Confirm join. The new machine appears in the device list after it restarts.
confirm.meshDescription: Once the new machine runs the command, confirm the join here. It appears in the device list after it restarts.
confirm.done: The new machine has joined; it appears in the device list after it restarts.

entry.title: Set up a public entry
entry.description: Open Settings → Remote access: Cloudflare Tunnel (named tunnel) gives you a fixed HTTPS address; Direct connection requires a fixed HTTPS entry you provide yourself.

status.quick: This is a temporary tunnel ({{url}}). Its address changes, so it is not suitable as a relay address — use a named tunnel or a direct connection instead.

hub.title: Make it the relay
hub.description: Open Settings → Multi-node Mesh, choose "Make this machine the Hub", enter the address from the previous step as the Hub public URL, create the first account and restart.
hub.warning: The Hub public URL cannot be changed afterwards. Decide on the final domain first.

status.self: This machine is already the Hub. Public address: {{url}}
status.node: This machine has already joined another relay ({{url}}), so it cannot be a relay itself.
status.mismatch: The Hub public URL does not match the current tunnel hostname; other machines may fail to connect.

hub.hintUseEntry: Enter the address from the previous step, {{url}}, as the Hub public URL.

invite.title: Connect other machines
invite.description: After installing tmex on other machines, follow "Join an existing relay" using a join token generated on this machine.
invite.ready: After installing tmex on another machine, switch to "Join an existing relay" to generate a join token here.

app.enforceHint: Validate Cf-Access-Jwt-Assertion on requests arriving through the tunnel and reject the ones that fail.

app.hostnameMismatch: This application covers a different hostname than the current tunnel, so token verification has no effect. Apply the rules again to bind it to the current hostname.

confirmRemove.title: Remove the Access application?

external.title: External reverse proxy
external.description: TLS is handled by Cloudflare Tunnel, nginx or Caddy in front of tmex.

selfsigned.title: Private CA
selfsigned.description: tmex issues its own certificate. Every device has to install the CA once.

acme.title: Let's Encrypt
acme.description: A publicly trusted certificate, renewed automatically. Needs a public domain name.

external.intro: tmex keeps serving plain HTTP and the proxy in front handles TLS. Point the proxy at the plain port and let it forward the original host, protocol and client address.
external.trustProxyHint: Turn this on only if tmex can be reached through your proxy alone.
external.trustProxyDetail: When on, tmex trusts X-Forwarded-Proto and X-Forwarded-For. Anyone who can reach the plain port directly could forge them, so keep that port closed.

selfsigned.intro: For a LAN or tunnel with no public domain. The private certificate authority (CA) never leaves this machine, and certificates are valid for 398 days.
selfsigned.sansHint: Hostnames or IP addresses you will type in the browser, up to 20. Anything not listed keeps showing a certificate error.
selfsigned.trustWarning: Browsers reject this certificate until the CA is installed. Install it on every device that opens this address.

guide.title: Install the CA on your devices
guide.intro: Download tmex-ca.crt, then follow the steps for your platform. Check the fingerprint above after installing.

macos.title: macOS
macos.steps: Double-click tmex-ca.crt to open Keychain Access, put it in the System keychain, then open the entry and set "When using this certificate" to "Always Trust".

ios.title: iOS / iPadOS
ios.steps: AirDrop or mail the file to the device and install the profile, then enable it under Settings → General → About → Certificate Trust Settings.

windows.title: Windows
windows.steps: Run certmgr.msc, go to Trusted Root Certification Authorities → Certificates → All Tasks → Import and pick tmex-ca.crt. Firefox keeps its own store, so import it there as well.

android.title: Android
android.steps: Settings → Security → Encryption & credentials → Install a certificate → CA certificate. The browser trusts user CAs; other apps only do so if they opt in.

linux.title: Linux
linux.steps: Copy the file to /usr/local/share/ca-certificates/tmex-ca.crt and run sudo update-ca-certificates (Debian/Ubuntu), or to /etc/pki/ca-trust/source/anchors/ and run sudo update-ca-trust (Fedora/RHEL).

acme.intro: Let's Encrypt issues a publicly trusted certificate for one domain. The domain must point at this machine; renewal runs automatically.
acme.domainHint: One hostname, no wildcards. It must already point at this machine.
acme.emailHint: Let's Encrypt uses it for expiry warnings.
acme.challengeHttpHint: Let's Encrypt reaches this machine on public port 80.
acme.challengeDnsHint: Uses the Cloudflare API instead. Works behind NAT and without port 80.
acme.cloudflareTokenHint: Needs Zone:DNS:Edit on the zone that holds this domain. Stored encrypted.

acme.stagingHint: Staging certificates are not trusted by browsers, but the rate limits are much looser. Use it while testing.
acme.pendingHint: Issuance runs in the background; this panel refreshes automatically.

hints.http01Linux: A user-level systemd service cannot bind port 80. Forward it on the router, or use DNS-01.
hints.dns01: The domain's DNS has to be managed by Cloudflare, with an API token that can edit its records.
